there is a tradeoff between average read performance and average write performance. To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.

The default strategy is to run a checkpoint once the WAL reaches 1000 pages and this strategy seems to work well in test applications on workstations, but other strategies might work better on different platforms or for different workloads.

claims.text: WAL separates write operations from the original database: changes are appended to a log file while the database file remains unchanged, allowing readers to access stable data while writers append changes. Unlike rollback journaling where both readers and writers must access the same database file, WAL enables simultaneous execution because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers.

claims.text: A long-running reader—such as a batch analytics job or background scan—prevents WAL checkpoints from completing because checkpoints must stop before any page accessed by an active reader. When checkpoints cannot complete, the WAL file grows unbounded, exhausting disk space and forcing all readers to scan an ever-larger WAL index. This failure is silent during single-threaded tests but emerges in production when latency-sensitive transactional writes coexist with background batch reads. The contents identify this as the most common production failure mode of the whole WAL subsystem.

claims.text: WAL's advantage over rollback journal disappears under sustained high concurrent reads. When multiple processes maintain overlapping read transactions continuously—with at least one reader always active—SQLite's checkpoints stall because checkpointing cannot proceed past pages readers are using. The WAL grows unbounded without resetting, and read latency rises with WAL file size, degrading performance to match or worse than rollback journal. This occurs when reader gaps never occur and the checkpoint has no opportunity to complete.

claims.text: WAL's write-speed advantage is offset by checkpoint cost and read-latency degradation as the WAL file grows. The throughput advantage narrows or reverses depending on checkpoint frequency: frequent checkpoints (every commit) maximize read performance but eliminate write acceleration, while infrequent checkpoints maximize write performance but degrade reads as the WAL grows. SQLite's default 1000-page threshold is calibrated for workstations but may harm performance on high-latency storage or read-heavy workloads where different checkpoint frequencies would be optimal.
